text.p: Pope John Paul will be travelling to Sarajevo this weekend to praise the city as a symbol of co-existence at a time when Bosnian Moslems are openly questioning whether multi-ethnicity is a realistic goal.
The Papal visit coincides with a public discussion on the previously taboo subject of carving out a purely Moslem state after a war which divided Bosnia-Herzegovnia along ethnic lines.
The debate was sparked by a series of articles in Sarajevo's main newspaper, Dnevni Avaz, considered the voice of the ruling Moslem political party.
"Is it time for Bosniaks (Bosnian Moslems) to think how to go on?" the paper asked in one issue.
With a new inter-ethnic government suffering from paralysis and refugees barred from returning to Serb or Croat-controlled territory, Moslem leaders are growing increasingly frustrated.
The U.S.-sponsored peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war in 1995 divided the country into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
A central government and parliament are supposed to govern the Serb republic and Moslem-Croat federation but in reality three national parties rule separate fiefdoms.

Diplomats say it remains unclear whether Moslem leaders are serious about building their own state or merely launched the discussion to test the political waters and grab the attention of distracted Western powers.
"This comes out of frusration because they're beginning to realise the world is not interested in Bosnia the way it once was," said one diplomat.
The Bosnian Moslem leadership, whose army controls less than 30 percent of the country, is facing a "real dilemma," said the diplomat, who asked not to be named.
"Do you forsake the Dayton accord and try to build on territory that you definitely control? Or do you decide to share power over a wider area but perhaps with less security"
Moslem leaders have officially denied that any division could ever be accepted. But some hint at the possibility of a military solution to capture territory now under Serb control.

A leading Sarajevo magazine reported that Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of the collective presidency, had formed a team of advisers to examine prospects for a Moslem state based on territorial swaps or possible military action.

On Wednesday, Izetbegovic's office confirmed the appointment of a council of advisers comprised of prominent Moslem politicians. But the president's aides denied the advisers would be drawing up plans for a separate state.
International mediators working to carry out the peace treaty say it is too soon to declare Bosnia dead.
They say much will depend on political developments in neighbouring Croatia and Serbia, where autocratic rulers have undermined Bosnia's reintegration.
Many Sarajevans still believe that co-existence among Moslems, Orthodox Christian Serbs and Catholic Croats is the only way forward and are especially receptive to the Pope's ecumenical message.
The papal visit carries important symbolism for Bosnia where relations between the three faiths are badly damaged.
"If the present trend continues it could lead to a radicalisation of Bosnian Moslems and their linking with militant Islamic movements," the daily Oslobodjenje wrote.
"All this gives a special dimension to the Pope's appearance in Sarajevo."
